cards.front: What are the three primary principles of anaerobic exercise prescription required when designing athletic resistance training programs?
cards.back:
The three core principles are:
  • Specificity: Training an athlete in a specific manner to produce a specific training adaptation or outcome.
  • Overload: Assigning a workout or training regimen of greater intensity than the athlete is accustomed to.
  • Progression: Systematically and gradually increasing the training stimulus over time to promote long-term adaptations.

cards.front: What is the SAID principle, and how does specificity apply to athletic movement patterns without requiring exact skill duplication?
cards.back: SAID stands for Specific Adaptation to Imposed Demands. The underlying principle dictates that the type of demand placed on the body determines the adaptation. Specificity applies to muscle groups, movement patterns, and contraction velocity, but does not require mimicking all aspects of a sporting skill (e.g., heavy squats recruit the same muscles as vertical jumping, despite differing movement velocities).

cards.front: What methods can a strength and conditioning professional use to apply the overload principle in resistance training?
cards.back:
Overload can be achieved by:
  • Increasing assigned exercise loads/resistance
  • Increasing weekly or daily training frequency
  • Adding exercises or sets to a workout
  • Emphasizing complex over simple exercises
  • Decreasing rest period lengths between sets and exercises

cards.front: How should the progression principle be applied in program design, and what is an example of a technical exercise progression?
cards.back: Progression must be introduced systematically and gradually based on the athlete's training status. An example of a technical exercise progression is advancing an athlete from learning the front squat to the hang power clean, and eventually to the power clean.

cards.front: What is a needs analysis, and what are the two main stages of this initial program design step?
cards.back:
A needs analysis is Step 1 of resistance training program design. It is a two-stage process consisting of:
  • Evaluation of the Sport: Determining the biomechanical, physiological, and injury requirements of the sport.
  • Assessment of the Athlete: Profiling training status, evaluating physical test results, and establishing primary resistance training goals.

cards.tag: Evaluation of the Sport: Three Core Analyses
cards.front: What three primary analyses must be conducted during the evaluation of the sport stage of a needs analysis?
cards.back:
The evaluation of the sport includes:
  • Movement Analysis: Body and limb movement patterns and specific muscular involvement.
  • Physiological Analysis: Priorities for strength, power, hypertrophy, and muscular endurance.
  • Injury Analysis: Common sites for joint and muscle injury and their causative mechanisms.

cards.front: What key muscles and physiological outcomes are identified in a needs analysis of the shot-put event?
cards.back: Shot-put is an all-body movement recruiting the triceps brachii (elbow extensors), deltoids (shoulder abductors), gluteals and hamstrings (hip extensors), quadriceps (knee extensors), and gastrocnemius and soleus (plantar flexors). It demands maximal strength and power alongside hypertrophy (to expand muscle cross-sectional area), with minimal muscular endurance demands.

cards.front: What four key factors must be evaluated when examining an athlete's training background or exercise history?
cards.back:
An assessment of training background includes examining:
  • Type of training program previously performed (sprint, plyometric, resistance)
  • Length of recent regular participation in previous training programs
  • Level of intensity involved in previous training
  • Degree of exercise technique experience and movement skill

cards.front: How are athletes classified across the training status continuum based on resistance training background (Table 17.1)?
cards.back:
Athletes are classified into three stages along a continuous spectrum:
  • Beginner (Untrained): Current training < 2–6 months; minimal or no technique experience.
  • Intermediate (Moderately Trained): Current training ∼ 2–6 months; basic technique experience.
  • Advanced (Trained): Current training ≥ 1 year continuous; high technique experience.

cards.front: Why should strength and conditioning professionals focus on only one primary resistance training goal per season (Table 17.2)?
cards.back: Focusing on one primary outcome (strength, power, hypertrophy, or muscular endurance) per season avoids conflicting cellular signaling pathways. Typically, hypertrophy or muscular endurance is prioritized in the off-season, strength and power in the preseason, and maintenance during the in-season.
